title: URL Shortener
problem: Design a URL shortener like TinyURL or bit.ly.
summary: A read-heavy service (about 10:1 read/write) that maps a short base62 code to a long URL and returns a 301/302 redirect. The design settles on base62 conversion over hash+collision-check: a distributed unique ID generator (per ) hands out monotonic 64-bit IDs; each ID is base62-encoded to 7 characters and stored alongside the long URL in a relational database, with a cache in front of reads. Sized for the book's target of 100M new URLs/day, 1160 writes/sec, 11.6K redirect QPS, 365B rows over 10 years, and ~365 TB total storage.

functional: POST /shorten accepts a long URL and returns a short code (generate one if none supplied, accept a custom alias if provided)
GET /:code issues an HTTP 302 redirect to the original URL with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 so every click reaches analytics
Codes are exactly 7 characters drawn from [0-9a-zA-Z] (base62), giving 62^7 ~= 3.5 trillion unique keys
Creation is idempotent per (user, longUrl) — the same input returns the same short code within a TTL window
Expired or revoked codes return 410 Gone so abuse teams can kill a link
Click events are emitted asynchronously to an analytics pipeline without blocking the redirect
nonFunctional: Handle 100M writes/day (~1.2K QPS average, 3.5K QPS peak) and 1B reads/day (~11.6K QPS average, 35K QPS peak)
Redirect p99 latency under 50ms end-to-end from the edge
99.99% availability for the redirect path; 99.9% for creation
10-year retention of 365B rows (~365 TB raw) with horizontal shardability
Durability: no lost short code once POST /shorten returns 201
Abuse: rate-limit anonymous creations to 10/minute/IP and scan long URLs against a malware blocklist

assumptions: Short URL char set = [0-9, a-z, A-Z] → 62 chars; length n chosen s.t. 62^n ≥ 365B → n = 7 (62^7 ≈ 3.5T)
estimates: Cache working set: top 20% of codes serve ~80% of reads → hot set ≈ 100M codes fit in a Redis tier

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> ratelimit[Rate Limiter] ratelimit --> api[Shortener API] api --> idgen[Unique ID Generator] api --> cache[(Cache)] api --> db[(Relational URL Store)]

client.name: Client (Browser / Mobile)
client.summary: Browser or mobile app that calls POST /shorten and follows GET /:code redirects.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- POST /shorten with a long URL, receive a short code
- GET /:code and follow HTTP 301/302 to the original URL
- Retry idempotent GETs on 5xx with small backoff

sections.heading: 301 vs 302
sections.body:
- 301 (permanent) is cacheable by browsers and CDNs — saves backend traffic but kills click analytics
- 302 (found) keeps every click visible to the backend. Most real services (bit.ly) use 302 for analytics.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client is where latency budgets begin. A 200ms end-to-end budget means every backend hop has to land under ~20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Browser caching of 301 redirects hides analytics and skews QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: If the service ever returns HTTP 301 (permanent) instead of 302, browsers and intermediary CDNs cache the Location header indefinitely. At 11.6K redirect QPS with a Pareto distribution (top 20% of codes = 80% of traffic), the hottest ~100M codes get cached client-side after first hit.
bottlenecks.symptom: Click counts drop 60–80% overnight after a 301 rollout; analytics dashboards show flat lines for popular links while backend logs show the same codes never re-requested. Cannot disable or revoke a short link because browsers won't re-check.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Standardize on HTTP 302 Found with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=0` (as already specified in the redirect flow). Add a response header lint in CI and a synthetic probe that asserts `Cache-Control: private, max-age=0` on every /:code response.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ratio of (redirect QPS at LB) / (unique codes seen per hour) — a sudden jump in cache-hit ratio at the browser layer shows up as this ratio climbing. Also alert if any response from /:code carries `Cache-Control: public` or `max-age > 0`.

bottlenecks.title: Retry storms on idempotent GET /:code amplifying backend load
bottlenecks.trigger: Client retries GETs on 5xx with 'small backoff'. During a partial outage (e.g., one API replica ejected, 0.05% baseline failure rate spiking to 5%), 11.6K QPS × 3 retries with no jitter = ~35K QPS — matching the peak capacity ceiling and leaving no headroom.
bottlenecks.symptom: Outages get worse instead of recovering: LB shows traffic 3x normal during incidents, API replicas CPU-saturate, healthy replicas get ejected under load, cascading to full tier failure. On-call sees 'retry amplification' pattern in LB logs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter (base 100ms, cap 2s, max 2 retries) in mobile SDK and JS client. Honor `Retry-After` header on 429/503. Add a client-side circuit breaker that stops retrying after 5 consecutive failures in 10s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track ratio of (LB request count) / (unique browser sessions) per minute; alert when ratio exceeds 1.3 (normal is ~1.05). Also alert on p99 retry count per session > 2 in RUM telemetry.

bottlenecks.title: DNS and TLS handshake dominate tail latency on first click
bottlenecks.trigger: Client flow budgets 2–8ms service time, but the first request from a cold client adds ~20–40ms DNS + ~50–100ms TLS handshake. For one-off clicks from email/SMS (common for shorteners), every request is effectively cold — affecting a large fraction of the 11.6K QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: p95 end-to-end latency reported by RUM is 150–250ms despite backend p95 under 10ms; users on mobile networks perceive short links as 'slow' even though server-side SLOs are green.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Serve the shortener domain from an anycast CDN edge with TLS 1.3 + 0-RTT resumption and HSTS preload. Publish short TTL (60s) DNS records from multiple resolvers. Consider HTTP/3 (QUIC) to collapse DNS+TLS+TCP into one RTT.
bottlenecks.detection: Instrument Navigation Timing API in a sample of browser sessions; alert if p95 of (responseStart - navigationStart) exceeds 120ms, broken down by TLS vs DNS vs TCP phase.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is called out in this design For a URL shortener, the "client" isn't just a passive browser — it's where the entire product experience lives. Every short link you've ever seen in an email, SMS, or tweet is activated by a browser following a redirect. That makes the client's behavior (how it handles 301 vs 302, how it retries on failure, how it caches DNS/TLS) a *design decision*, not an implementation detail. The system is explicitly built around the assumption that clients will honor `Cache-Control: private, max-age=0` on 302 responses so every click reaches the backend for analytics. ## What happens if you ignore the client Suppose the API accidentally returns HTTP 301 (permanent redirect) instead of 302. Browsers and corporate proxies will cache the `Location` header essentially forever. The user experience looks fine — links still work — but the operator sees click analytics flatline overnight, and revoking a malicious link becomes impossible because millions of browsers never re-check. The failure didn't happen in the API or the database; it happened in a component the team forgot to treat as part of the system. ## A concrete number The design targets 11,600 redirect QPS, peaking around 35K. If even 10% of clients retry once on a transient 5xx with no jitter, you add 1,160 QPS of pure amplification — and during an incident that ratio climbs fast. That's why the client spec mandates exponential backoff with jitter and a max of 2 retries. ## Trade-off Treating the client as a first-class component means shipping and versioning SDK behavior (backoff, headers) — more coordination, but the only way to keep backend SLOs honest.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer distributing traffic across stateless API replicas.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin with least-connections fallback. Healthy pool only; ejection after 3 consecutive 5xx within 10s.

sections.heading: TLS termination
sections.body: Terminates TLS at the LB; plaintext HTTP to the API tier inside the VPC. Saves ~3–5ms per request.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- LB itself is the choke point — deploy in an HA pair with anycast or ELB multi-AZ.
- A misbehaving API replica is ejected before users notice; they may see one extra retry.

gained: Fine-grained retry, timeout, and circuit-breaker policy
lost: Higher operational complexity (control plane)
Slightly higher per-hop CPU
Weaker service-discovery integration
Manual reload for config changes unless using plus

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturates at 35K peak redirect QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: The LB terminates TLS for 100% of traffic. At peak 35K redirect QPS + 3.5K shorten QPS ≈ 38.5K new TLS handshakes/sec in the worst case (email/SMS clicks are mostly cold connections without session resumption). Each RSA-2048 or ECDHE handshake costs ~1-3ms of CPU; at this rate a single LB node exhausts cores before hitting the 50K concurrency ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegs at 100%, p99 request latency climbs from ~2ms to 100-500ms, new TCP connections queue or get RST, and downstream API replicas appear underutilized while clients see timeouts. On-call sees 'connection reset' errors in RUM but healthy backends.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT session resumption and session tickets (cuts handshake cost ~70%), offload to hardware TLS (AWS NLB/ALB, or dedicated TLS accelerators), and size the LB pool on handshakes/sec not just bandwidth. Budget 2x headroom: provision for ~80K handshakes/sec across the HA pair.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 60% sustained for 2min, TLS handshake rate > 20K/sec per node, and tls_handshake_duration_p99 > 10ms. Track session-resumption hit ratio; alert if it drops below 70%.

bottlenecks.title: Aggressive health-check ejection cascades under partial API degradation
bottlenecks.trigger: Ejection policy is '3 consecutive 5xx within 10s.' At 35K peak QPS spread over ~20 API replicas = ~1750 QPS per replica. A replica seeing a transient 0.5% error rate hits 3 consecutive 5xx in well under a second and gets ejected. Remaining 19 replicas absorb +5% load each; if 2-3 replicas flap, the surviving pool runs at >115% capacity and cascades.
bottlenecks.symptom: Pool size oscillates (replicas ejected, re-added, ejected again), upstream_rq_pending_total climbs, tail latency doubles, and the LB reports healthy_upstream_count bouncing between 15-20. On-call sees 'thundering herd' on freshly re-added replicas.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use outlier detection with a minimum healthy pool floor (e.g., never eject more than 30% of the pool), require 5 consecutive failures over 30s instead of 3/10s, and add slow-start (gradual traffic ramp) on re-admission. In Envoy: outlier_detection.max_ejection_percent=30, success_rate_minimum_hosts=5.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on healthy_upstream_count < 0.7 * total_upstream_count, ejection_rate > 1/min, or any replica ejected+readmitted more than twice in 10min (flapping indicator).

bottlenecks.title: Single-AZ LB becomes the system's blast radius
bottlenecks.trigger: The design notes 'deploy in an HA pair with anycast or ELB multi-AZ' but an HA pair in one AZ is a single failure domain. At 11.6K sustained / 35K peak QPS, AZ loss drops 100% of traffic until DNS failover (TTL 60s) propagates — during which ~700K-2M redirects fail.
bottlenecks.symptom: Total outage window of 60-300s during an AZ incident; synthetic monitors show 100% error rate; client retry storms (per the client component's retry-amplification bottleneck) hit the surviving AZ at 3x normal load on recovery, causing secondary overload.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy LB across 3 AZs behind an anycast VIP (AWS Global Accelerator or GCP global LB) with health-based withdrawal, not DNS failover. Each AZ sized for 2x peak (70K QPS) so any one AZ can absorb full traffic. Pre-warm connection pools on standby AZs.
bottlenecks.detection: Continuous multi-region synthetic probes with alert on any regional probe failure > 30s; track per-AZ QPS balance (alert if any AZ carries > 50% of total, indicating uneven failover); measure DNS failover time quarterly via game-days.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a load balancer in front of a URL shortener For a URL shortener, the overwhelming majority of traffic is dumb, fast redirects — every short link in every email, tweet, and SMS turns into a `GET /:code` that must land on *some* healthy server in under ~10ms. A single API box can't hold that traffic, and even if it could, it would be a single point of failure: one crash and every short link on the internet pointing at your domain goes dark. The LB exists so the API tier can be a *pool* of stateless, interchangeable replicas that you can add, remove, or lose without users noticing. ## What breaks without it Without an LB, clients resolve your domain to one IP. If that box is saturated, users see connection timeouts; if it dies, DNS TTLs mean a 60–300 second outage while records propagate. The API tier can't be scaled horizontally in any useful way — you can run 20 replicas but traffic only hits one. TLS also has to terminate on every API box, burning CPU that should be serving redirects, and a single bad deploy takes the whole service down because there's no pool to eject an unhealthy replica from. ## The number The design targets **11,600 redirect QPS sustained, ~35K at peak**. At ~5ms service time per request, one API replica safely handles ~200 concurrent requests, so peak alone needs 35,000 / 200 ≈ **175 replicas** running in parallel. Something has to fan 35K incoming connections across those 175 boxes and eject the ones returning 5xx — that's the LB's whole job. ## Trade-off You accept the LB itself as a new failure domain (hence the HA pair across AZs) in exchange for being able to scale and heal the API tier independently.

api.name: Shortener API
api.summary: Stateless Go/Java service that owns POST /shorten and GET /:code.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /shorten { url } → { code, short_url }
GET /:code → 302 → long url
```

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body:
1. Validate URL (scheme, length, blocklist)
2. Ask ID generator for next base62 id
3. INSERT into URL store (code → long_url, created_at, owner)
4. SETEX code in Redis (TTL 24h)
5. Return short URL

sections.heading: Read path
sections.body:
1. GET code from Redis (hit rate target ≥ 95%)
2. On miss, SELECT from URL store and backfill cache
3. Emit click event to analytics (async, non-blocking)

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU. With peak 35K QPS and ~5ms service time, ~200 concurrent reqs/replica → 20 replicas at safe utilization.

lost: Cold starts add 50–300ms p99
Redis/DB connection churn hurts tail latency

bottlenecks.title: Dedup SELECT on long_url turns every write into a full-table lookup
bottlenecks.trigger: The shorten flow (Figure 8-7 step 2) runs `SELECT short_url FROM urls WHERE long_url =?` before every INSERT. At 1,160 writes/sec sustained (peak ~3.5K) against a 365B-row / 365 TB table, this query is unserveable without an index on long_url — and a B-tree index on a VARCHAR(2048) column at that scale is enormous (likely >2 TB) and hot on every write.
bottlenecks.symptom: POST /shorten p99 climbs from ~20ms to 200ms+ as the table grows; DB primary CPU and IOPS saturate on index lookups; write QPS ceiling drops below the 3.5K peak target; cascading timeouts cause the API tier's 5000-concurrency budget to fill with blocked writers, starving reads that fall through on cache miss.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace the equality SELECT with a hash-based lookup: store `long_url_sha256` (32 bytes) as a secondary index or a separate `long_url_hash → short_url` KV table (Redis or a dedicated Cassandra table). Alternatively, drop dedup entirely (accept that the same long URL may get multiple codes — bit.ly does this) and document the trade-off. If dedup must stay, shard the lookup by hash prefix.
bottlenecks.detection: Track p99 latency of the dedup SELECT as a separate metric from the INSERT; alert when it exceeds 10ms or when long_url index size exceeds 80% of buffer pool. Monitor ratio of (dedup hits) / (writes) — if <5%, the cost isn't worth it.

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous analytics emit blocks the redirect hot path under broker backpressure
bottlenecks.trigger: The read path calls `analytics.emit_async(code, user_ip, ts)` before returning 302. At 35K peak redirect QPS, that's 35K events/sec into Kafka/Kinesis. If the async client's in-memory buffer fills (broker slowdown, partition rebalance, network blip), the 'async' call silently becomes blocking — or drops events, but typically blocks first. With 5000 concurrency budget and ~5ms service time, a 50ms analytics stall collapses throughput to ~100K/sec ceiling instantly.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redirect p99 jumps from ~10ms to 100–500ms with no corresponding Redis or DB latency spike; API replica CPU drops (threads blocked on I/O) while concurrency metric pegs at 5000; on-call sees 'healthy' backends but climbing 502s from the LB as the API tier refuses new connections.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a bounded in-memory ring buffer with a drop-oldest policy (never block the request thread). Producer config: `max.block.ms=0`, `buffer.memory` sized for 10s of traffic (~350K events), background flusher thread. On buffer full, increment a dropped_events counter and return 302 anyway — analytics loss is acceptable, redirect latency is not.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on analytics_emit_latency_p99 > 5ms (it should be <1ms for a true fire-and-forget), analytics_buffer_fullness > 70%, and dropped_events_per_sec > 0. Dashboard redirect p99 alongside analytics emit p99 to correlate incidents.

bottlenecks.title: Redis connection pool exhaustion on cold-cache fleet restart
bottlenecks.trigger: Each API replica maintains a Redis connection pool (typically 50–200 conns). With 20 replicas at steady state, ~2K connections total. After a coordinated deploy or Redis failover, all 20 replicas simultaneously see 100% cache miss; at 35K QPS that's 35K concurrent DB reads plus 35K Redis SETEX backfills, exceeding the 500-concurrency DB ceiling ~70x. API replicas queue requests, hit their 5000-concurrency cap, and start rejecting.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-deploy or post-failover: redirect p99 spikes to seconds, 503s at the LB, DB primary CPU at 100%, API replica concurrency pegged at 5000 with requests queuing. Recovery is slow because each timed-out request didn't warm the cache, so retries also miss.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement request coalescing (singleflight pattern) on the miss path — per replica, only one in-flight DB read per code; other concurrent requests for the same code wait on the same future. Add a DB-side concurrency limiter (semaphore capped at 300 of the 500 budget, leaving headroom). On deploy, use rolling restarts with Redis connection pre-warming. Consider a small in-process LRU (10K entries) as an L1 in front of Redis to blunt the thundering herd.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache_hit_ratio dropping below 90% for >30s (normal target ≥95%), db_concurrent_queries > 400, and api_replica_concurrency > 4000. Track singleflight_coalesced_requests/sec — a sudden spike indicates a hot-key miss storm.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Shortener API is here The API is the brain of the URL shortener. Everything else in this design — the ID generator, the cache, the database — is a dumb specialist that only does one thing. Something has to sit in the middle and orchestrate them: validate the long URL on `POST /shorten`, ask the ID generator for a fresh number, base62-encode it, write the row, warm the cache, and return the short link. On `GET /:code` it has to check Redis first, fall through to the DB on a miss, backfill the cache, and fire off an analytics event without blocking the 302. None of those steps belong in the load balancer, the database, or the client. ## What happens without it If you wired the LB straight to Redis and the DB, the client would have to know the base62 scheme, call the ID generator itself, handle cache misses, and decide when to backfill. Every mobile app and browser would need to ship that logic — and the moment you changed the blocklist or the cache TTL, you'd be stuck waiting for users to update. Worse, there'd be nowhere to enforce URL validation, so anyone could INSERT garbage rows directly into your 365 TB table. ## The number At peak **35K redirect QPS** and ~5ms service time, each API replica safely handles ~200 concurrent requests (5000 / ~25ms worst case). That's 35,000 / 200 ≈ **175 replicas** — only possible because the API is stateless and horizontally scalable; all the state lives behind it in Redis and the DB. ## Trade-off You accept an extra network hop (~3–15ms) in exchange for a single place to evolve business logic.

idgen.name: Unique ID Generator (base62 conversion)
idgen.summary: Distributed generator that hands out unique numeric IDs; the API base62-encodes each ID to a 7-character short code.

sections.heading: Book's recommendation
sections.body: The book explicitly chooses **base62 conversion** over hash+collision-check: a distributed unique ID generator (per, Snowflake-style) returns a 64-bit integer; the API converts it to base62 — e.g. ID `2009215674938` → `zn9edcu`. 62 chars = [0-9, a-z, A-Z]; length n = 7 because 62^7 ≈ 3.5T ≥ 365B.

sections.heading: Why not hash + collision resolution
sections.body: Hash (CRC32/MD5/SHA-1) truncated to 7 chars produces collisions that force a DB existence check on every write, plus a retry loop on collision. Book compares both approaches in Table 8-3 and settles on base62 for correctness + simplicity.

sections.heading: Implementation notes
sections.body: Each API replica fetches a block of IDs from a central counter (or embeds a Snowflake library per ). Local handout is lock-free.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Range-server outage: each API replica has ~1–10K ids buffered; absorbs minutes of downtime.
- Double-issued block after split-brain: mitigated by fencing tokens on the counter.

alternatives.name: Hash + collision resolution (MD5/SHA-1 truncated to 7 chars)

gained: Deterministic: same long URL → same short code (free dedupe)
lost: Extra DB existence check on every write
Collision retry loop tails under high write QPS
Book explicitly rejects this for the final design
Larger IDs → longer base62 codes under some layouts
Clock skew can cause duplicates
Write throughput bounded by single primary
Hard to shard later

bottlenecks.title: Central counter becomes write-path SPOF at 3.5K peak shorten QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: If the ID generator is implemented as a single central counter (e.g., a Redis INCR or a DB sequence) rather than Snowflake-in-process, every one of the 1,160 sustained / 3,500 peak POST /shorten calls must round-trip to it. With ~175 API replicas each requesting IDs, one slow node or network blip adds latency to 100% of writes. At 3.5K QPS a single Redis instance handling INCR tops out around 80–100K ops/sec in theory but practically saturates on network+persistence long before, and any failover (30–60s) halts all writes globally.
bottlenecks.symptom: POST /shorten p99 jumps from ~20ms to hundreds of ms or times out entirely; writes across all API replicas fail simultaneously during counter failover; on-call sees 'idgen.next timeout' errors uniformly across the fleet with no correlation to a specific replica.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use block allocation: each API replica fetches a range of 1,000–10,000 IDs at a time and hands them out lock-free in-process. A replica crash wastes at most one block (acceptable given 62^7 = 3.5T address space). Alternatively, use Snowflake-style in-process generation (per book ) eliminating the network hop entirely. Run the central counter as an HA pair with fencing tokens to prevent double-issue on split-brain.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on idgen_request_latency_p99 > 5ms, idgen_block_exhaustion_events/min > 0 (indicates replicas fetching blocks faster than expected), and any idgen.next failure rate > 0.01%. Track per-replica id_buffer_remaining; alert if any replica's buffer drops below 100 IDs.

bottlenecks.title: Base62 code length assumption breaks if ID generator emits non-monotonic 64-bit values
bottlenecks.trigger: The design fixes short codes at 7 characters because 62^7 ≈ 3.5T ≥ 365B expected rows. But a 64-bit Snowflake ID (timestamp + machine + sequence) can reach values > 62^10 ≈ 8.4 × 10^17 almost immediately — a Snowflake ID from 2024 base62-encodes to ~11 characters, not 7. If the generator is wired in naively, every short code becomes 10–11 chars from day one, breaking the product's 7-char promise and any client/UI assumption.
bottlenecks.symptom: First short URLs emitted in production are 'https://sho.rt/2pQr9mZxA8k' instead of the advertised 'sho.rt/zn9edcu'; marketing/product complains links look ugly; any fixed-width DB column (VARCHAR(7)) rejects inserts with 'data too long for column short_url'; client SDKs truncating to 7 chars silently corrupt codes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a compact monotonic counter (start at 0, ++) rather than Snowflake for ID allocation — book explicitly recommends this so base62(id) stays ≤ 7 chars for the full 365B row lifetime. If Snowflake is required for other reasons, either widen short_url to VARCHAR(11) and accept longer codes, or apply a bijective compression (e.g., map timestamp+seq into a dense 41-bit space before base62).
bottlenecks.detection: Add a CI assertion that base62(idgen.next) has length ≤ 7. Alert in production on any INSERT into urls where LENGTH(short_url) > 7, and on distribution of code lengths emitted per hour (should be tightly clustered 6–7 chars).

bottlenecks.title: Block-allocated IDs waste address space and leak sequential order
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1,160 writes/sec and a 10K block size per replica, 20 replicas reserve 200K IDs but only consume ~1,160/sec collectively. Every deploy (rolling restart every few days) abandons ~90% of each replica's unused block. Over 10 years at ~100 deploys/year, waste can reach 10–50% of the 3.5T address space — still within budget but erodes the 7-char headroom. Additionally, monotonic IDs make short codes guessable: `zn9edcu` → `zn9edcv` likely exists, enabling enumeration attacks on private/unlisted URLs.
bottlenecks.symptom: Address-space utilization grows faster than the 365B row count suggests; security researchers or scrapers enumerate adjacent short codes to discover private links; after many years, base62 codes start ticking into 8 characters unexpectedly.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shrink block size to 1,000 (reduces waste to <1% at this QPS) and add a background reclaim job that returns unused tail ranges on graceful shutdown. For enumeration resistance, apply a keyed bijective permutation (e.g., Feistel cipher over 42-bit space) to the ID before base62 encoding — preserves uniqueness and 7-char length while making codes unguessable.
bottlenecks.detection: Track (max_issued_id / total_rows) ratio monthly; alert if it exceeds 1.5 (indicates >33% waste). Monitor id_block_abandoned_count per deploy. For enumeration: alert on 404 rate for /:code patterns where requested codes are sequential neighbors of recently-issued codes.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the ID generator is here For a URL shortener, every new long URL needs a short code that is **guaranteed unique** — if two users ever got the same code, one of them would silently get redirected to the wrong site. The obvious alternatives both break down at this scale: hashing the long URL (MD5, SHA-1 truncated to 7 chars) produces collisions that force a "does this code already exist?" check on every write plus a retry loop, and a database auto-increment column bottlenecks all writes through a single primary. The ID generator solves uniqueness *before* the row ever reaches the database, by handing out monotonic 64-bit integers that the API then base62-encodes into the 7-character code. ## What happens without it Imagine the API just picks random 7-character strings. At 1,160 writes/sec, collisions are rare at first but grow as the table fills — and every write now costs a `SELECT` to check, then maybe a retry, then another check. Write p99 climbs from ~20ms to hundreds of ms, and under peak load (3.5K QPS) the database's index on `short_url` becomes the hottest thing in the system. Users see shorten requests time out; operators see the DB primary CPU-bound on existence checks. ## The number The design targets **365 billion rows over 10 years**. Base62 with 7 characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion possible codes — roughly 10× headroom. A monotonic counter walks that space densely and deterministically, so every ID fits in 7 chars without ever colliding. ## Trade-off Sequential IDs are guessable (enumeration attacks on private links), which the designer accepts as the cost of avoiding collision-retry loops.

cache.name: Redis Cache
cache.summary: In-memory KV cache for hot code → long URL mappings.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body: Key `u:{code}` → long URL string. TTL 24h. Pareto distribution: top 20% of codes get ~80% of reads, so the working set is bounded even as total URLs grow.

sections.heading: Eviction policy
sections.body: `allkeys-lru` at 80% memory watermark. Capacity: 50 GB fits ~100M hot codes at ~500B each.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Cold cache after restart → p95 spikes to ~15ms until warm (DB fallthrough).
- Hot-key stampede: use request coalescing in the API or Redis `GETEX` with short negative cache.

gained: Slightly lower latency on pure GETs
lost: No persistence / replication
No data structures (Sorted Sets, Streams, Pub/Sub)
Not shared between API replicas → lower hit ratio
Invalidation across replicas is hard

bottlenecks.title: Cold-cache thundering herd after Redis failover or restart
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis primary failover, node restart, or eviction flush wipes the hot set of ~100M codes. At 11.6K sustained / 35K peak redirect QPS, 100% of reads miss simultaneously and fall through to the DB, which is sized for only 1,160 writes/sec with a 500-concurrency ceiling — a 70x overload instantly.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redirect p99 spikes from ~5ms to seconds; DB primary CPU pegs at 100%; API replica concurrency pegs at 5000 with request queuing; LB returns 503s; cache_hit_ratio drops from ~95% to near 0% and recovers slowly over minutes as the working set re-warms one miss at a time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run Redis in a replicated cluster (primary + 2 replicas per shard) with automatic failover via Sentinel/Cluster so reads survive a single-node loss. Enable AOF or RDB persistence so restarts don't start cold. Add request coalescing (singleflight) in the API to collapse concurrent misses for the same code into one DB read. Pre-warm the cache after planned restarts by replaying the top-N hot codes from access logs.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache_hit_ratio < 90% sustained for >30s (target ≥95%), redis_connected_slaves < expected count, and db_read_qps > 3x baseline. Track redis_uptime_seconds and alert on unexpected resets.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key concentration saturates a single Redis shard
bottlenecks.trigger: Pareto distribution: top 20% of codes serve 80% of reads, but within that, a viral link (e.g., a trending news URL) can draw a disproportionate share — realistically 5–20% of all traffic on a single key. At 35K peak QPS, one hot code can drive 2–7K GETs/sec at a single Redis shard while other shards sit near idle. A single Redis instance handles ~100K ops/sec but network egress on one key at ~500B payload × 7K QPS ≈ 28 Mbps from one key alone, and CPU on that shard climbs disproportionately.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis node shows CPU at 80%+ while siblings are at 10–20%; GET latency p99 for that node climbs from <1ms to 5–15ms; client-side latency histogram shows bimodal distribution; `redis-cli --hotkeys` or MONITOR reveals one code dominating traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a small in-process LRU (10K entries, ~1s TTL) in front of Redis on each API replica — collapses hot-key reads to ~1/sec/replica regardless of client QPS. Alternatively, replicate hot keys across multiple shards with a suffix-based sharding scheme (`u:{code}:{0..7}`) and randomize the suffix at read time. Monitor and rebalance shards if skew persists.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard cpu_utilization variance > 3x across the Redis cluster, per-key ops/sec > 1000 (via `redis-cli --hotkeys` sampled every 5min), and per-shard network_out_bytes showing >2x the cluster median.

bottlenecks.title: Working set outgrowing the 50 GB memory budget, causing LRU churn
bottlenecks.trigger: Capacity is sized for ~100M hot codes at ~500B each = 50 GB. But long_url averages 100B and overhead (Redis dict, TTL metadata, expiry hashes) adds ~200–300B per entry — realistic per-entry cost is 400–600B. As total URLs grow toward 365B over 10 years, even the 20% 'hot' set drifts upward; a marketing campaign, news event, or crawler hitting a broader tail of codes can push the active working set past 100M entries.
bottlenecks.symptom: allkeys-lru eviction rate climbs from near-zero to thousands/sec; cache_hit_ratio slowly drops from 95% to 85–90%; DB fallthrough QPS doubles or triples; redirect p95 creeps up from ~5ms toward 10–15ms; `INFO memory` shows `used_memory` pinned at maxmemory with `evicted_keys` ticking steadily.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard Redis horizontally (Redis Cluster with 4–8 shards) so total memory scales linearly; size for 2x headroom (100 GB+ usable). Tune TTL down from 24h to 6–12h for codes with only 1–2 recent hits (adaptive TTL based on access frequency). Use Redis `OBJECT ENCODING` to keep values as embstr where possible. Monitor and expand capacity proactively before eviction storms start.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_evicted_keys_per_sec > 100 (normal should be near 0 with well-sized cache), used_memory / maxmemory > 0.85, and cache_hit_ratio dropping below 93% over a 1h window. Track working-set size via `MEMORY USAGE` sampling.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis sits in front of the database here For a URL shortener, the read pattern is brutally lopsided: people click links constantly but rarely create new ones (10:1 read/write). Every redirect is basically the same question — "what long URL does `aZ3kP9q` point to?" — and the answer never changes once the code is created. Hitting a sharded relational store for each of those lookups would waste the database's most expensive resource (disk I/O and connection slots) on work that a simple in-memory key→value lookup can do in under a millisecond. ## What breaks without it Without Redis, every redirect falls through to the URL store. The DB tier is sized for ~1,160 writes/sec with a 500-concurrency ceiling — it is *not* sized to absorb 11.6K reads/sec on top of that, let alone the 35K peak. You'd see redirect p99 climb from ~5ms into the tens of milliseconds, DB CPU pegged, and connection pools exhausted. Users perceive "slow links"; on-call sees a saturated primary and starts scrambling to add read replicas (expensive, stateful, slow to provision) instead of just scaling a stateless cache tier. ## The number Pareto kicks in hard: the design assumes the **top 20% of codes serve ~80% of reads**. At 11.6K redirect QPS, that's ~9,280 QPS concentrated on a hot set of ~100M codes — which fits comfortably in a 50 GB Redis tier at ~500 bytes/entry (100M × 500B = 50 GB). So one cache layer absorbs 80% of read traffic that would otherwise pound the database. ## Trade-off You accept a second datastore to operate (and cold-cache risk after failover) in exchange for keeping the DB sized for writes, not reads.

db.name: Relational URL Store
db.summary: Durable relational database (sharded MySQL/Postgres) keyed by id, with a unique index on shortURL.

sections.heading: Data model
Why relational (not an in-memory hash table)
sections.body: Book explicitly rejects an in-memory hash table for real systems — 'memory resources are limited and expensive'. A relational DB gives durability, indexes on `short_url`, and easy replication/sharding.

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: Shard by `id` or `hash(short_url)` so reads and writes spread uniformly. At 365 TB / N shards, size each shard to fit SSD. Book wrap-up calls out 'Database replication and sharding are common techniques'.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: Short codes are immutable after creation, so reads can go to a read replica with eventual consistency. Primary handles writes (much lower QPS: 1160 vs 11.6K).

gained: Linear write scaling and multi-DC replication out of the box
lost: Book uses a relational model for clarity
Operational complexity if you don't already run Cassandra
Costly at 365 TB storage
Vendor lock-in

bottlenecks.title: Dedup SELECT on long_url scans a 365 TB table without a viable index
bottlenecks.trigger: The shorten flow (Figure 8-7 step 2) runs `SELECT short_url FROM urls WHERE long_url =?` before every INSERT. At 1,160 sustained / 3,500 peak writes/sec against a table growing to 365B rows / 365 TB over 10 years, a B-tree index on VARCHAR(2048) long_url exceeds 2 TB — far larger than any realistic buffer pool, forcing disk I/O on most lookups.
bottlenecks.symptom: POST /shorten p99 climbs from ~20ms to 200–500ms as the table grows; DB primary IOPS and CPU saturate on index page reads; write throughput ceiling drops below the 3.5K peak target; API replica concurrency pegs at 5000 with blocked writers, causing cache-miss reads to queue behind them.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace the raw equality lookup with a hash index: add `long_url_sha256 BINARY(32)` column with a unique/secondary index (~12 KB per 365 rows vs 2+ KB/row for the raw string), or offload dedup to a separate `hash(long_url) → short_url` Redis/Cassandra KV table. Alternatively drop dedup entirely (bit.ly does — same long URL can get multiple codes) and save the write amplification.
bottlenecks.detection: Track p99 latency of the dedup SELECT as a distinct metric from INSERT; alert when it exceeds 10ms, when long_url index size exceeds 80% of buffer pool, or when disk_read_iops on the primary exceeds 50% of provisioned IOPS during write bursts.

bottlenecks.title: 500-concurrency primary ceiling collapses under cache-miss storms
bottlenecks.trigger: The DB is sized for 500 concurrent queries — sufficient for steady-state 1,160 writes/sec + ~580 miss-path reads/sec (at 95% cache hit ratio on 11.6K QPS). But a Redis failover, restart, or mass eviction drops hit ratio to 0%, sending 35K peak QPS straight at the DB — a 70x overload against the 500-concurrency cap.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache_hit_ratio drops below 90%; DB connection pool exhausted with wait_count climbing; query p99 jumps from ~10ms to seconds; API replicas return 503s as their own 5000-concurrency budget fills with requests queued on DB; recovery is slow because timed-out reads never backfill the cache.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add request coalescing (singleflight) at the API layer so concurrent misses for the same code collapse to one DB read. Deploy Redis as a replicated cluster with persistence (AOF) so failover doesn't start cold. Provision read replicas (≥4) behind a read-only endpoint to absorb cold-cache bursts; short codes are immutable so eventual consistency is safe. Cap DB-bound concurrency per API replica (semaphore) at 15–20 to prevent herd amplification.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on db_active_connections > 400, db_connection_wait_time_p99 > 50ms, cache_hit_ratio < 90% for >30s, and db_read_qps > 3x baseline. Track singleflight_coalesced_requests/sec as a leading indicator of miss storms.

bottlenecks.title: Sharding by id creates hot-shard skew for recently-issued codes
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding by id (monotonic from the generator) means all new writes land on the single shard owning the current ID range. At 1,160 sustained / 3,500 peak writes/sec, one shard absorbs 100% of INSERTs while older shards see only reads. Worse, newly created URLs are disproportionately read (recency bias in sharing), so the newest shard also serves a tall fraction of the ~580 cache-miss reads/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: One shard shows 3–5x CPU and IOPS vs siblings; write p99 on the hot shard climbs while other shards idle at 10–20% utilization; rebalancing lags; storage growth is uneven (one shard fills to 80% while others sit at 30%), forcing premature resharding of the hot node.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard by `hash(short_url)` or `hash(id)` instead of raw id, so writes and reads spread uniformly across N shards regardless of issue order. If monotonic id sharding is required for range scans, use a consistent-hash ring or pre-split the current range into M virtual shards and randomize assignment. Size each shard to fit SSD (e.g., 24 shards × 15 TB at the 10-year mark).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard write_qps or cpu_utilization variance > 3x across the cluster, per-shard storage_used variance > 2x, and per-shard p99 query latency spread > 5x the cluster median. Re-evaluate shard key if skew persists after rebalance.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a durable database sits behind the cache For a URL shortener, the short code → long URL mapping has to live *forever* (or at least 10 years per the design). Redis is fast but it's a cache — it evicts entries under memory pressure, loses data on restart without persistence, and is sized for only the hot 20% of codes. If `sho.rt/aZ3kP9q` was created three years ago and hasn't been clicked in a week, it's gone from Redis. Someone still needs to answer "what does this code point to?" when it's clicked tomorrow. That someone is the relational store: the durable, authoritative record of every short URL ever issued. ## What breaks without it Without a durable store, every Redis eviction is permanent data loss. A user creates a link, shares it in an email, and a month later it 404s because the cache entry expired. The operator sees climbing 404 rates with no clear cause; marketing complains that links "randomly die." There's also nowhere to recover from: a Redis cluster failure wipes the entire product. The API tier can't help — it's stateless. The ID generator can't help — it only hands out new IDs, it doesn't remember old ones. ## The number The design targets **365 billion rows across 10 years = 365 TB of storage**. That volume cannot fit in a 50 GB Redis tier (it's 7,300× too big), and it absolutely cannot fit in RAM economically. It has to live on sharded SSDs behind an indexed table, which is exactly what the relational store provides. ## Trade-off You accept ~10ms disk-backed reads (vs Redis's ~1ms) on the ~5% cache-miss path in exchange for durability and effectively unlimited capacity.

ratelimit.name: Rate Limiter
ratelimit.summary: Per-IP / per-user throttle that protects the write path from abuse.

sections.heading: Why it's here
sections.body: 'A potential security problem we could face is that malicious users send an overwhelmingly large number of URL shortening requests. Rate limiter helps to filter out requests based on IP address or other filtering rules.' —.

sections.heading: Placement
sections.body: Sits between the load balancer and the API tier. Token-bucket in Redis keyed by IP (or user id if authenticated). Requests above the limit get 429 Too Many Requests.

sections.heading: Typical policy
sections.body:
- Anonymous IP: 60 shorten/min, unlimited redirects.
- Authenticated: 600 shorten/min.
- Global cap: 3× peak write QPS to prevent traffic spikes from overwhelming the ID generator.

bottlenecks.title: Redis token-bucket shard becomes a write-path SPOF at peak shorten QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Every POST /shorten (1,160 sustained / 3,500 peak QPS) performs a Redis INCR+EXPIRE (or Lua script) against the bucket keyed by client IP. A single Redis node handles ~80–100K ops/sec in theory but practically saturates on CPU and network well before that — and any failover (10–30s) or network partition blocks 100% of writes system-wide, since the rate limiter sits inline between the LB and the API.
bottlenecks.symptom: All POST /shorten requests across every API replica hang or return 5xx simultaneously during a Redis blip; on-call sees 'ratelimit.check timeout' errors uniformly with no correlation to a specific API replica; write-path p99 jumps from ~20ms to seconds; redirects stay healthy (they bypass the limiter), making root cause non-obvious.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run the rate-limit Redis as a replicated cluster (primary + 2 replicas with Sentinel) sharded by hash(client_ip) across 3+ nodes so no single node carries all 3.5K peak QPS. Implement fail-open behavior: on Redis timeout >50ms, allow the request and increment a 'ratelimit_degraded' counter rather than blocking writes. Use a local in-process token bucket as L1 that only consults Redis every N requests or on bucket-near-empty.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ratelimit_redis_latency_p99 > 5ms, ratelimit_redis_errors/sec > 0, ratelimit_degraded_fail_open_events/min > 0, and any single Redis shard CPU > 60% sustained. Track per-shard ops/sec variance — alert if any shard carries >2x the cluster median.

bottlenecks.title: Per-IP keying is defeated by NAT'd traffic and CGNAT, blocking legitimate users
bottlenecks.trigger: The policy caps anonymous IPs at 60 shorten/min. Mobile carriers and corporate proxies route tens of thousands of users behind a single egress IP (CGNAT). A moderately popular consumer app embedding shorten calls from mobile clients easily drives one carrier IP past 60/min even with normal usage — far below the 3,500 peak QPS global budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Support tickets spike from users on specific mobile carriers or corporate networks reporting 'shorten is broken, getting 429' while the overall system shows healthy write QPS well under capacity; ratelimit_429_rate climbs for a small set of /24 subnets; authenticated users on the same network are unaffected (600/min limit, or user-id keyed).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Key anonymous buckets by (IP, User-Agent-hash) or a browser-issued anonymous cookie rather than IP alone. Maintain an allowlist of known CGNAT ranges (published by major carriers) with a 10x higher limit. Prefer authenticated user-id keying whenever a session cookie is present. Return `Retry-After` headers so clients back off cleanly instead of retrying into the limit.
bottlenecks.detection: Track 429 rate grouped by /24 CIDR; alert when any single /24 produces >1% of total 429s (indicates shared-NAT false positives). Monitor ratio of distinct User-Agents per IP — IPs with >100 distinct UAs/hour hitting 429 are almost certainly NAT.

bottlenecks.title: Limiter bypass on redirect path leaves /:code unprotected against scraping and enumeration
bottlenecks.trigger: Policy states 'Anonymous IP: 60 shorten/min, unlimited redirects.' At 35K peak redirect QPS the design assumes benign traffic, but monotonic base62 IDs (per the idgen component) make codes enumerable. A scraper walking `aaaaaaa` → `zzzzzzz` at 10K QPS from a single IP is indistinguishable from organic traffic to the limiter and can exfiltrate the entire URL corpus or discover private/unlisted links.
bottlenecks.symptom: 404 rate on /:code climbs to 30–60% driven by sequential-neighbor probes; DB read QPS elevated despite cache hit ratio staying normal (scrapers hit cold entries); one or two source IPs account for a disproportionate share of redirect traffic; security team reports private links appearing in external crawlers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a separate, looser redirect-path limit (e.g., 1,000/min per IP, 10K/min per /24) that catches only egregious scrapers without impacting normal clicks. Detect enumeration patterns: alert when an IP's 404 rate exceeds 20% over 5 min or when requested codes are sequential neighbors. Combine with the idgen mitigation to apply a keyed bijective permutation so codes are unguessable.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-IP 404_rate > 20% sustained 5min; per-IP redirect_qps > 500 (well above any realistic human click rate); ratio of sequential-neighbor-code requests / total redirects > 0.01. Log top-N source IPs by redirect QPS hourly.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the rate limiter is here For a URL shortener, the write path is uniquely attractive to abusers. Every `POST /shorten` burns a globally unique 64-bit ID, an INSERT into a 365 TB table, and a Redis warm-up — all for a payload a spammer can generate in microseconds. A script spraying shorten requests at full line-rate from a handful of IPs can easily push 50K+ writes/sec at a system provisioned for **1,160 sustained / 3,500 peak**. Without a gate in front of the API, the ID generator, the DB primary's write concurrency, and the dedup-lookup index all get pushed past their limits by traffic that isn't even real users. ## What happens without it A spam campaign creating shortened links for phishing domains floods `POST /shorten` at 20K QPS from a botnet. The API's 5000-concurrency budget fills with writers queued on the DB; legitimate users creating a single link see the POST hang for seconds or time out. Meanwhile, redirects (reads) slow down too because the API replicas shared between reads and writes are saturated. On-call sees DB write p99 at 500ms, ID-generator buffer churn, and a table growing by millions of junk rows per hour that now live in the 365 TB store forever. ## The number At the **3,500 peak shorten QPS** budget, a per-IP limit of 60/min means a single IP consumes at most 1/sec — so it takes **3,500 distinct IPs acting in concert** to reach peak, instead of one script. That's the whole point. ## Trade-off You accept false positives on NAT'd mobile carriers in exchange for a bounded write path.

operations.title: Redirect short URL (cache hit — hot path)
operations.name: Redirect short URL (cache hit — hot path)
operations.description: A user clicks a short link. 95%+ of the time the code is already in Redis and the API returns a 302 in under ~10ms.

steps.title: User clicks https://sho.rt/aZ3kP9q
steps.action: Browser initiates GET request to the shortener domain. The path segment after the host is the base62 short code.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /aZ3kP9q HTTP/1.1
Host: sho.rt
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
steps.note: DNS resolution and TCP/TLS handshake happen here too but are cached after the first request.

steps.title: Load balancer picks an API replica
steps.action: The LB terminates TLS, inspects the Host header, and forwards the plaintext request to the healthiest API replica via round-robin (least-connections fallback).
steps.codeOrCommand:
# conceptual routing decision
upstream = pool.pick(algo="round_robin", healthy_only=True)
forward(req → upstream)

steps.title: API extracts short code, queries cache
steps.action: The API router matches GET /:code, extracts "aZ3kP9q", and issues a single Redis GET on the cache key before ever touching the database.
steps.codeOrCommand:
code = req.path.strip("/") # "aZ3kP9q"
long_url = redis.get(f"u:{code}") # single round trip

steps.title: Redis returns the long URL (cache HIT)
steps.action: Redis looks the key up in its in-memory hash table — O(1), sub-millisecond. The key exists because this code has been accessed in the last 24h (TTL).

steps.title: API builds 302 response
steps.action: API constructs an HTTP 302 Found with the long URL in the Location header. A click event is dispatched asynchronously to analytics — it does NOT block the response.

steps.title: LB relays the response back
steps.action: Load balancer re-wraps the response in TLS and sends it to the client. No routing decision needed — this is the return path of an established connection.

steps.title: Browser follows the redirect
steps.action: Receiving a 302, the browser automatically issues a new GET to the Location URL. Total perceived latency: client → server → client, typically 20–50ms depending on geography.
steps.codeOrCommand:
// Browser behavior (not our code)
window.location = response.headers.Location

operations.title: Redirect short URL (cache MISS — falls through to DB)
operations.name: Redirect short URL (cache MISS — falls through to DB)
operations.description: Same redirect but the code isn't in Redis. API reads from the URL store, backfills the cache, and returns. p95 is noticeably higher.

steps.title: User clicks https://sho.rt/zX9mN2p
steps.action: A less popular code — either new, or evicted from Redis after 24h TTL.

steps.title: LB forwards to API
steps.action: Same L7 routing as the hot path.

steps.title: API checks Redis first
steps.action: API tries the cache as always. It doesn't know yet that the key is missing.

steps.title: Redis returns nil (cache MISS)
steps.action: The key doesn't exist. Redis responds with nil in well under a millisecond — misses are just as fast as hits.

steps.title: API reads from URL store
steps.action: Cassandra single-row GET by partition key. Fast (3–10ms) but an order of magnitude slower than Redis.

steps.title: API backfills the cache (async, fire-and-forget)
steps.action: API writes the entry to Redis with a 24h TTL so the next access is a hot-path hit. This is dispatched in parallel with preparing the response — it does NOT add latency to the user.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# async, does not block response
redis.setex("u:zX9mN2p", 86400, long_url)

steps.title: API builds 302 response
steps.action: Same as the hot path — 302 with Location header.

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path through the load balancer.

steps.title: Browser follows redirect
steps.action: Cold-path total latency is typically ~15–30ms — still fast, but 3–5x the hot path. This is why the cache is so valuable.

operations.title: Shorten a long URL (write path)
operations.name: Shorten a long URL (write path)
operations.description: POST /shorten — ID generator issues a new code, DB persists the row, Redis is warmed, short URL returned.

steps.title: User submits a long URL
steps.action: The user pastes a long URL and hits Shorten. The browser POSTs it as JSON to the API.

steps.title: LB forwards to the rate-limiter / API tier
steps.action: Same routing as the read path. POSTs are not sticky — any replica can handle them.

steps.title: Rate limiter checks the client's token bucket
steps.action: Before the write path burns an ID, the rate limiter confirms the caller is under quota. Over quota → 429 Too Many Requests. Redirects bypass this check.
steps.codeOrCommand:
allowed, remaining = bucket.consume(key=client_ip, cost=1)
if not allowed: return 429, {"error": "rate_limited"}

steps.title: API validates and checks for existing longURL
steps.action: API validates URL, then checks if this exact longURL is already in the database. Per Figure 8-7, if it exists, return the existing shortURL. If not, fall through to get a new ID.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if not url.startswith(("http://", "https://")): return 400
if len(url) > 2048: return 400
if blocklist.contains(domain(url)): return 403 # Book Figure 8-7 step 2: dedup check
existing = db.query("SELECT short_url FROM urls WHERE long_url =?", url)
if existing: return 200, {"short_url": existing} # Not present — get a new ID from generator
id = idgen.next

steps.title: ID generator returns a unique 64-bit ID; API base62-encodes it
steps.action: Book example: generator returns ID `2009215674938`; base62 conversion yields `zn9edcu`. Each API replica keeps a buffer of IDs fetched from the generator; handout is lock-free and sub-millisecond.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Step 4 (Figure 8-7): get a globally unique ID
id = idgen.next # e.g. 2009215674938 # Step 5 (Figure 8-7): base62 conversion
def base62(n): alpha = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ" s = while n > 0: s.append(alpha[n % 62]) n //= 62 return "".join(reversed(s)) code = base62(id) # → "zn9edcu"

steps.title: API persists (id, short_url, long_url) row — Figure 8-7 step 6
steps.action: Single-row INSERT into the relational urls table. Book Table 8-4 shows the three-column layout: id, shortURL, longURL.
steps.codeOrCommand:
INSERT INTO urls (id, short_url, long_url)
VALUES (2009215674938, 'zn9edcu', 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_design');

stateAfter.durability: committed to primary + replicated to read replicas

steps.title: API warms the cache (parallel with response)
steps.action: The new code is written to the cache with 24h TTL so subsequent redirects hit cache immediately. Fire-and-forget from the API's perspective — the response does not wait for it.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# async, parallel to response
redis.setex("u:zn9edcu", 86400, long_url)

steps.title: API returns the short URL
steps.action: Response body includes the short code and the full short URL.

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client shows the short URL
steps.action: User gets https://tinyurl.com/zn9edcu — ready to share. End-to-end write latency typically 15–40ms.

tradeoffs.rationale: A unique-ID generator guarantees zero collisions so the write path needs no retry loop, and 7-char output is predictable.
302 with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 forces every click to reach the backend, preserving analytics and enabling link revocation.
Workload is single-key point lookup by short_code with no range scans; a covering index on one column wins on cost and operational familiarity.

tradeoffs.decision: Write-through cache vs lazy cache population
tradeoffs.chosen: Write-through on create, lazy on read miss
tradeoffs.rationale: Newly created links are often clicked within seconds; populating on write avoids a cold miss, and TTL expiry handles eviction.

tradeoffs.decision: Synchronous click logging vs async Kafka fire-and-forget
tradeoffs.rationale: Analytics must never block the redirect — a lost click is cheaper than a 500ms p99 regression.
Aliases are a premium feature with abuse risk, so gate them behind a logged-in user and reserve a separate alias namespace.

interviewFollowUps.question: How do you prevent two users from racing to claim the same custom alias under concurrent POST /shorten requests?
A customer reports that a short link still works after they revoked it — walk me through all the places that URL could be cached and how you invalidate each.
How would you extend this to support per-user click analytics dashboards with sub-second freshness?
The Snowflake service goes down. Design a fallback that keeps the write path live without double-issuing an ID.
Scale the design 10x to 1B new links per day — where does it break first and what do you change?
How do you detect and throttle a spammer who rotates across 10,000 IPs to create malicious short links?
